documents.unit: Rutgers Office of Information Technology (all campuses)
documents.title: Guidance on the use of AI at Rutgers
documents.summary: Universitywide IT guidance (shared by all three campuses) with five short sections: use approved AI tools, academic integrity, confidential data, reviewing AI output, and purchasing. Coursework rules are left to instructors, with a fallback that AI is not permissible unless stated.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single stance: it says guidance "will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor" and that students must follow "their program and instructors' guidance". It adds a default that AI "should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated", but this is a fallback, with no tiers, so the decision is delegated to instructors.

units.why: "provides access to generative AI tools with protections for use in university work" says OIT supplies licensed, sanctioned AI tools to the university community, so it is P17; it states a fact about what is provided, hence informs, and it is addressed to all users.
units.anchor: provides access to generative AI tools with protections for use in university work
units.resolution_why: Coder A set actor all and unit_stance encourage; coder B set actor admin and unit_stance permit. The sentence says OIT "provides access" to tools "for use in university work", so it speaks to everyone who may use them, not to administrators: actor all. It makes tools available without recommending their use, so permit rather than encourage. Both coders chose P17, informs, general.
units.fit_note: Also says the licensed tools come with security and privacy safeguards; the type is about a sanctioned tool and does not capture the safeguards.

units.why: "your data will not be used to train the models underlying the tools" states a privacy protection of the approved versions, which explains why vetted tools are preferred (P50); it is a statement of fact, so informs.
units.anchor: your data will not be used to train the models underlying the tools

units.why: "only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used at the university" directs everyone to use vetted tools to protect data, so P50 (prefer vetted tools); it is a recommendation ("should") that restricts use to approved tools.
units.anchor: only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used at the university
units.fit_note: Type says prefer vetted tools; this says only approved tools should be used, a restriction on all university use.

units.why: "guidance on the appropriate use of AI tools in academic settings will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor" leaves the academic-use decision to instructors (P04); it describes how rules work, so informs.
units.anchor: guidance on the appropriate use of AI tools in academic settings will typically vary

units.why: "Faculty should consider providing guidance to students on the use of AI" asks instructors to communicate AI expectations, though only as something to consider, so nearest type P09 with a fit note.
units.anchor: Faculty should consider providing guidance to students on the use of AI
units.fit_note: Type requires a statement; this only says faculty should consider giving guidance.

units.why: "students are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors" tells unsure students to check expectations with the instructor, so P10.
units.anchor: students are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors

units.why: "should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated" sets a fallback rule of no AI when instructors are silent, so P06 (fallback), not P01, because it is conditional on instructor communication.
units.anchor: they should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors

units.why: "Students are responsible for understanding and abiding by their program and instructors' guidance or rules on the use of AI" puts the duty of knowing and following local AI rules on students. It is a student duty that applies throughout coursework (general), "responsible" is mandatory (must), and no existing type says this.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for understanding and abiding by their program and instructors
units.frag_end: rules on the use of AI.
units.resolution_why: Coder A chose P29 (general) with a fit note; coder B chose UNCOVERED (during-work). P29 means students own the work they submit; this sentence makes students responsible for knowing and obeying their instructors' AI rules, which the source does not tie to submitted work. Stretching P29 would lose a recurring kind of policy, so UNCOVERED. Phase is general because the sentence states a standing duty, not an action at a point in the work.
units.uncovered_note: Students are responsible for knowing and following their program's and instructors' AI rules.

units.why: "the student's own and created without the aid of impermissible technologies, materials, or collaborations" says coursework must be the student's own work and made without impermissible technology, so it fits P29 (submitted work must be their own); it is stated as what academic integrity requires, so must, with a restricting effect.
units.anchor: the student’s own and created without the aid of impermissible technologies, materials, or collaborations
units.frag_start: the principles of academic integrity require
units.resolution_why: Coder A chose P36 (misconduct); coder B chose P29 (during-work). The passage says "principles of academic integrity require that students ensure that coursework be the student's own", a rule about owning submitted work (P29). P36 needs unauthorized AI use to be classified as misconduct; the page only quotes the integrity principle and never says that AI misuse is misconduct. Phase is general because the quote states a principle, not a step in the work.
units.fit_note: Frames own-work as a requirement of the Academic Integrity Policy and bars "impermissible technologies"; the page does not say that AI misuse is misconduct.

units.why: "Confidential information, Protected Health Information (PHI), and other proprietary Rutgers information may not be appropriate for use in AI applications" warns users against entering sensitive data into AI tools, which is P50; the hedge "may not be appropriate" makes it should-not.
units.anchor: Protected Health Information (PHI), and other proprietary Rutgers information may not be appropriate for use
units.fit_note: Hedged ("may not be appropriate") and about confidential and proprietary university information.

units.why: "please consult this data classification chart for AI tools" directs users to a chart that shows which data may go into AI tools, so it supports protecting confidential data (P50); it asks to consult, hence should.
units.anchor: please consult this data classification chart for AI tools
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder B (P77, topic privacy-data). The sentence is a real instruction to consult a data-classification chart for AI tools, so it is kept. The chart exists to decide what data may be used with AI, which is P50 (protect confidential data); P77 is for AI use that must follow existing law or policy, and the next clause naming the Information Classification Policy is only a reference. Final type P50, should.
units.fit_note: A pointer to a classification chart and to the Information Classification Policy, not a rule in itself.

units.why: "Always review and verify AI content and outputs" is a direct instruction to check AI output, P31; "Always" makes it must and it applies to all users while working.
units.anchor: Always review and verify AI content and outputs

units.why: "AI tools can produce biased and inaccurate information" names bias and inaccuracy as risks, which fits P53 (name bias, harms); it states a fact, so informs.
units.anchor: AI tools can produce biased and inaccurate information
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded one unit for "biased and inaccurate information, and may include copyrighted information without attribution" (P53); coder B split it into two units. Bias and inaccuracy and the copyright risk are different statements, so they are split into two units here. This unit keeps the bias and inaccuracy clause as P53, as both coders did.
units.fit_note: Type is about bias, harms and environmental cost; this mentions bias and inaccuracy only briefly.

units.why: "may include copyrighted information without attribution" warns that AI output can carry copyrighted material, a copyright concern that fits P52; it is a statement of risk, so informs.
units.anchor: may include copyrighted information without attribution
units.resolution_why: Found by coder B as a separate P52 unit; coder A folded this clause into its P53 unit with a fit note and rejected P52 because no ownership rule is stated. The clause is its own risk statement, so it is kept as its own unit. P52 (copyright of AI output) is the nearest type and the fit note records the gap.
units.fit_note: Warns of copyrighted content without attribution; the type is about licensing and ownership of outputs, and the page states no ownership rule.

units.why: "You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content used for university work" makes the user answerable for what they use, so P29; "responsible for" is must, and it applies to every user.
units.anchor: You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content
units.fit_note: Responsibility is for the accuracy and appropriateness of AI content used in university work by any user, not only for submitted student work.

units.why: "you must follow the same security processes and risk assessments as for other software purchases" sets a review step before an AI application is bought, which is a vendor-review rule (P65); it is binding ("must") and addressed to those buying for the university, so admin, at the set-up stage.
units.anchor: you must follow the same security processes and risk assessments as for other software purchases
units.frag_start: If you are considering the purchase of an AI
units.policy: Anyone considering purchasing an AI application for use at Rutgers must follow the same security processes and risk assessments as for other software purchases, as well as standards for digital accessibility.
units.resolution_why: Coder A chose P76, admin, before-course; coder B chose P65, all, before-course. The sentence requires the security process and risk assessment used for software purchases, i.e. institutional review of an AI vendor product before adoption, which is what P65 covers; P76 is for how AI is used in operations, which the sentence does not describe. The "you" is a university buyer (department or staff), so actor admin, as coder A had it. Coder B's normalized policy is kept because it follows the source.
units.fit_note: Covers purchase review via security risk assessment and digital accessibility standards, not data-sharing limits with providers; P76 (operational AI use) is the close alternative.

units.why: The list of the Academic Integrity, Information Classification and Acceptable Use policies, said to be "particularly relevant for the use of AI at Rutgers", points AI use to existing university policies (P77); it is informational, so informs.
units.anchor: are particularly relevant for the use of AI at Rutgers
units.resolution_why: Found only by coder A. Coder B instead coded the descriptions of three listed policies as three separate units (P36, P77, P77). The sentence "are particularly relevant for the use of AI at Rutgers" is the AI statement and is kept as one P77 unit. The one-line descriptions of each linked policy ("Outlines the standards for classifying information...", "Details on standards of academic integrity...", "Outlines the acceptable use of university information technology resources...") say nothing about AI, so they are dropped.
units.fit_note: Names existing policies as relevant but does not say AI misuse falls under them.

notes: Single universitywide OIT page shared by all Rutgers campuses; no Camden-specific, school or computing documents found. Course layer deferred. Reconciled from two coders; no new types proposed by either coder.
